title: Secure a Multi-Agent AI Coding Pipeline (DevSecOps / Enterprise AI Architect)

teaser.setup: Your org wants autonomous AI coding agents (plan → write code → open PRs → deploy) wired into the SDLC. Security, compliance, and platform all need to sign off. Design the guardrails and defend the hard trade-offs — how do agents ship code without becoming your biggest attack surface?
you_will_practice: Where agents get autonomy vs where a human gates the change
Securing the agent supply chain: prompts, tools, secrets, and models
DevSecOps controls in an agent-driven pipeline (SAST/DAST, policy-as-code)
Compliance evidence and audit for AI-authored changes
Responding to a prompt-injection-driven pipeline compromise

sample_node.prompt: How much autonomy does a coding agent get in the pipeline?
sample_node.model: Give agents autonomy to propose (write code, open a PR, run tests in a sandbox) but gate the state changes — merge to protected branches, prod deploy, IAM/policy edits — behind human approval and the same required checks a human PR faces. Autonomy scales the cheap, reversible work; a human (or a stricter policy gate) owns the irreversible, high-blast-radius steps. The boundary is drawn by reversibility and blast radius, not by trust in the model.
signals: separates propose from irreversible actions
gates by reversibility / blast radius
agent PRs face the same checks as humans

n1.prompt: Before any pipeline diagram: what do you clarify, and what's the shape of a secure agent-driven SDLC in a paragraph?
n1.model: Clarify: which SDLC steps agents touch (design, code, review, deploy?), what's regulated (SOX/change control, PII/HIPAA), the blast radius of a bad change, and who is accountable for an AI-authored change. Shape: agents run in a sandboxed, least-privilege execution environment; they can propose changes as PRs but every change flows through the same gated pipeline as human work — SAST/secret-scan/dependency-scan, required review, policy-as-code, signed artifacts — with full provenance that the change was AI-authored. A human or a hard policy gate owns merges to protected branches and prod. Treat the agent's tools, prompts, and retrieved context as an attack surface.
signals: clarifies regulated steps + accountability first
agents propose, the gated pipeline enforces
provenance that a change is AI-authored

n2.prompt: How much autonomy does a coding agent get in the pipeline?

options.label: Propose only: agent writes code + opens PRs, humans gate merges/deploys
options.note: scales cheap work, humans own irreversible steps

options.label: Fully autonomous: agent merges and deploys to prod on green tests
options.note: fast, but no gate on irreversible/high-blast-radius changes

options.label: Agent has admin/CI credentials so it can 'fix things end to end'
options.note: dangerous — a compromised agent = compromised pipeline

n2b.prompt: Defend or correct that autonomy choice under a security review.
n2b.model: Full autonomy to merge and deploy — or handing an agent standing admin/CI credentials — fails review: a single prompt-injection or model mistake now ships to prod, and the agent becomes the highest-value target in your estate. Correct it: agents get least-privilege, short-lived credentials scoped to propose-and-test in a sandbox; irreversible/high-blast-radius steps (protected-branch merge, prod deploy, IAM changes) stay behind human approval or a hard policy gate, with the same required checks a human faces. Draw the boundary by reversibility and blast radius, never by how much you trust the model.
signals: irreversible steps stay gated
least-privilege, short-lived agent credentials
boundary = reversibility/blast radius, not trust

n3.prompt: An agent reads an issue, a dependency's README, and CI logs as context. How do you stop a prompt-injection from turning the agent into an insider threat?
n3.model: Treat ALL retrieved/tool content (issues, repo files, dependency docs, logs, web) as untrusted data, never instructions — the classic injection defense. Keep the agent least-privilege so even a hijacked agent can only propose, not merge/deploy/exfiltrate. Constrain tools to an allowlist with typed, validated arguments; no arbitrary shell/network egress. Run the agent in an isolated sandbox with egress controls so it can't phone home with secrets. Scan agent-authored diffs for injected secrets/backdoors before they reach review. Log every tool call for audit.
signals: external content is data, not instructions
least-privilege limits blast radius of a hijack
tool allowlist + sandbox + egress control + audit

n4.prompt: Security asks about the agent's own supply chain: prompts, tools, and the model. What do you lock down?
n4.model: Version and review system prompts and tool definitions like code (in git, PR-reviewed) — a prompt change is a security-relevant change. Pin and vet the models/providers behind a gateway; no team points an agent at an unvetted model. Pin tool and dependency versions; scan them (the agent shouldn't be able to add an arbitrary dependency without the same dependency-scan a human faces). Sign build artifacts and generate an SBOM so an AI-authored build is as traceable as any other. Rotate the agent's credentials and keep them short-lived.
signals: prompts + tool defs are versioned, reviewed code
models pinned/vetted behind a gateway
dependency scanning + SBOM + signed artifacts

n5.prompt: Where do you shift security left so a bad agent change is caught before prod, not after?
n5.model: Same gated pipeline for agent and human PRs: SAST + secret scanning + dependency/SCA scan on every diff, DAST against a staging deploy, and policy-as-code (OPA/Conftest, IaC scanning) so a change that violates a control is blocked automatically rather than caught in review. Required status checks + required reviewers on protected branches. Canary/progressive deploy with automated rollback so even an approved-but-bad change is limited and reversible. The controls are automated gates, not a reviewer's good intentions.
signals: SAST/secret/SCA + DAST in the pipeline
policy-as-code blocks violations automatically
canary + automated rollback limits a bad change

n6.prompt: How do you handle secrets and permissions so the agent never becomes a credential-harvesting machine?
n6.model: The agent never sees long-lived secrets: use short-lived, workload-scoped credentials (OIDC federation to CI, a secrets manager with just-in-time, narrowly-scoped tokens) issued per run and revoked after. Least privilege — the agent's identity can open a PR and run sandboxed tests, nothing more; deploy/IAM permissions belong to the gated deploy stage, not the agent. Secret-scan agent output so it can't embed a leaked key in a diff. Egress controls prevent exfiltration. Every credential use is audited.
signals: short-lived, scoped credentials (OIDC/JIT), no standing secrets
agent identity is least-privilege (propose, not deploy)
secret-scan output + egress control + audit

n7.prompt: Audit and compliance need to sign off on AI-authored changes (change control, SOX, regulated data). What evidence do you produce?
n7.model: Provenance on every change: who/what authored it (agent + version + prompt version), the model used, the inputs/context, the reviews and required checks that passed, and the approver of any gated step — an immutable, auditable trail. Change-control records treat an agent PR like any change: linked ticket, reviewer, test evidence, rollback plan. Data handling: agents working on regulated code/data run under the same classification, masking, and residency rules; retrieved context is logged. Human accountability is explicit — an approver owns the merge, so 'the AI did it' is never the answer. Map controls to the framework (SOX change control, SOC 2, etc.).
signals: immutable provenance + audit trail per change
agent changes go through normal change-control
explicit human accountability + framework mapping

n8.prompt: Incident: a poisoned dependency README injected instructions, an agent opened a PR that quietly weakened an auth check, and it slipped through into prod. Walk the response.
n8.model: Contain first: roll back the deploy (canary/automated rollback), revoke the agent's credentials, and freeze agent-authored merges. Assess blast radius: what shipped, what data/auth was exposed, which other agent PRs share the poisoned context. Eradicate: remove the poisoned dependency, patch the auth check, rotate any exposed secrets. Then the real fix is systemic, not 'tell the agent to be careful': the injection worked because external content was trusted and a bad change wasn't gated — so tighten tool/egress controls, add the missing policy-as-code check and required auth-path review, and add a regression test. Blameless postmortem, and update the threat model. Prevention is a control, not a prompt.
signals: contain (rollback + revoke) before root-causing
systemic fix: gating/policy/controls, not 'prompt the agent better'
blameless postmortem + updated threat model + regression test

n9.prompt: Where did you grant the agent power without naming the control that contains it, the trade-off, or how you'd prove it to an auditor?
checklist: I drew the autonomy boundary by reversibility/blast radius, not model trust
I treated all retrieved/tool content as untrusted data, not instructions
I versioned and reviewed prompts + tool definitions like code
I gave the agent least-privilege, short-lived credentials only
I made security an automated gate (SAST/SCA/policy-as-code), not a hope
I produced an auditable provenance trail with explicit human accountability
I fixed the incident systemically, not by 'prompting the agent better'

recommend.label: DevOps for AI — CI/CD, IaC, canary/rollback
